terms.definition: A chain of blocks of transactions, each block committing to the one before it.
A shared record more than one party keeps. A blockchain is one design for that record.
A short fingerprint of a longer input. The same input always gives the same fingerprint. A small change gives a different one.
A tree of hashes, so a small proof can show that one item sat inside a large set.
A key you can publish. Other people use it to check a signature or to derive an address.
The secret that authorises a signature. Whoever can use it can act as that key.
Software or hardware that holds keys and builds transactions. The assets stay on the ledger.
Who can move the asset, and under what rule.
Multi-party computation: a signature made by several parties without any one of them holding the whole key.
A rule that more than one key must sign before a spend.
A hardware security module: a device that holds key material and performs signing inside a boundary.
How a network chooses one history when more than one is possible.
The right to propose a block is bought with computation that anyone can check.
The right to propose or vote is tied to an asset that can be penalised.
The point after which a block is not expected to be replaced.
A program the ledger will run, with the result written into the shared state.
The rules for how contract code executes and how it is metered.
A bridge from a fact outside the chain to a value inside it.
A mechanism that lets an asset or a message be represented on another system.
Execution happens off the base chain. A proof or a challenge window connects the result back.
Whether the contents of a block were actually published, not just the header.
A proof that a statement is true without revealing why, beyond what the statement itself says.
A token that aims to track a reference unit, usually a currency.
A bank deposit represented as a token, still a claim on that bank.
A central-bank liability in digital form, if and when that central bank issues one.
A token that claims to track an asset or a cashflow that exists off the ledger.
Representing a defined claim as a transferable record.
A node allowed to propose or vote on blocks under the protocol's rule.
A receipt token for stake that has been delegated, so the receipt can move while the stake stays locked.
Using the same stake, or a receipt for it, as security for an additional service.
A penalty that destroys or confiscates stake when a validator breaks a stated rule.
A network that pays operators for a physical service: coverage, storage, energy, sensors.
A signed statement about a subject, which the subject can present later without the issuer being online.
Know your business: evidence of who owns and controls a company, collected before you rely on it.
An identifier a subject can prove control of, without a single registry being the only issuer.
A key or an account that software may use, inside a budget and a policy set by a person or a firm.
The moment an obligation is discharged, not the moment a message is sent.
A pool that quotes a price from a formula and its balances, instead of from an order book.
Assets pledged so that a debt can be repaid if the borrower does not pay.
A promise or a mechanism that aims to keep a price near a reference.
Software that checks a chain by headers and proofs, without replaying every transaction.
Value that can be extracted by choosing the order of transactions, or by inserting around them.
Letting an account's validation rule be code, rather than a single signature.
A meter for computation and storage, paid so that a program cannot run forever for free.
An exchange of two assets where either both transfers complete or neither does.
